contents.title: Reading: When an institution reports what is believed rather than what is known
contents.body:
## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about impersonal reporting passives require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
Within an economic policy unit drafting a briefing before official statistics are released, a seemingly straightforward question became an exercise in judgment rather than procedure. The central responsibility belonged to the senior economist, Dalia Mourad. The decision was how to refer to market expectations that have not yet been confirmed by published data. The issue mattered because an early decision would shape what colleagues, stakeholders, and later reviewers treated as the working interpretation. A premature conclusion could create momentum that was difficult to reverse, while excessive caution could delay a useful response. The group therefore treated the wording of the decision as part of the decision itself: what it said needed to reflect not only preference, but what the available information could actually support. Two strands of evidence carried most weight. First, several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. Second, business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. Their convergence made it difficult to dismiss the issue as a one-off impression, yet the group resisted the easy leap from consistency to certainty. The strands did not necessarily measure the same construct, and neither automatically established a single causal explanation. Their real value lay in the pattern they formed and in the sharper questions that pattern allowed reviewers to ask. The main caveat was substantial: the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. A limitation of this kind does not necessarily invalidate the underlying evidence; it changes what the evidence is entitled to support. The reviewers therefore replaced the crude question ‘Is the evidence good or bad?’ with a more useful one: ‘What is this evidence good enough to show?’ That distinction matters whenever a reliable dataset is narrow, a credible witness has only partial access, or a coherent model remains sensitive to assumptions that are open to challenge. A credible counter-position also had to be represented: one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. The group did not include this view as a ceremonial concession before returning to its preferred answer. Members tested whether the objection changed the interpretation of the evidence, the cost of acting, or the cost of waiting. In several parts of the discussion, the counterargument narrowed the wording and sharpened the conditions attached to the recommendation. That made the final position more defensible because the strongest alternative explanation had been answered rather than caricatured. The practical outcome was measured rather than dramatic: the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators. Just as important, the decision contained a theory of revision. If later evidence challenged the assumptions, the organization would have a defined reason to reconsider instead of defending the earlier position merely for consistency. Colleagues could also see which part of the conclusion rested on direct evidence, which part was inferential, and which part represented a judgment about acceptable risk. That transparency reduced the chance that a cautious claim would later be remembered as a categorical promise. The wider lesson is that reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. Language contributes directly to that discipline. A reporting verb can imply endorsement or distance; a conditional can distinguish a real possibility from a remote hypothetical; a focusing structure can correct a mistaken assumption; and a nominal phrase can either package a familiar concept efficiently or conceal the agent who acted. Complexity is therefore not the goal. The relevant question is which formulation makes the logic, stance, and information structure most accurate for the audience and genre. For anyone facing a similar problem, the practical task is drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. A strong response keeps the distinctions that matter, acknowledges uncertainty without becoming evasive, and remains readable enough for another person to act on. The result is not merely a more advanced piece of English. It is a better record of how a decision was reached and what would justify changing it.

## Key words
| Word | Meaning | Example |
| is thought to | يُعتقد أنه | The briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to. |
| is understood to | يُفهم أنه | The unit uses “is understood to” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |
| is estimated to | يُقدَّر أنه | The unit uses “is estimated to” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |
| impersonal passive | مبني للمجهول غير شخصي | Do not use an impersonal passive to disguise weak evidence as institutional consensus. |
| source-neutral | محايد تجاه المصدر | The team discussed the source-neutral because it affected how the evidence and final decision should be interpreted. |

## Comprehension
1. What decision did the senior economist, Dalia Mourad need to make?
2. What was one important strand of evidence?
3. What second strand of evidence supported the discussion?
4. What was the main limitation?
5. What counter-position had to be considered?
6. What practical outcome was reached?

## Answers
1. how to refer to market expectations that have not yet been confirmed by published data
2. several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter
3. business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized
4. the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters
5. one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view
6. the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators

contents.title: Listening: Can we say the figure is expected to fall?
contents.body:
## Before you listen
- Listen for the distinction between evidence, limitation, counterargument, and recommendation.
- Notice how the speakers calibrate certainty and disagreement rather than presenting every point categorically.

## Transcript
A: We need to settle the question of how to refer to market expectations that have not yet been confirmed by published data. What do you see as the strongest evidence?
B: The first point is that several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. That is more than a single impression.
A: Agreed. Is there independent support, or are we still relying on one type of evidence?
B: There is a second strand: business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. I would treat the combination as meaningful, though not automatically conclusive.
A: What is the strongest reason not to go further in the wording?
B: The main limitation is that the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. That affects how broadly we can generalize the conclusion.
A: A counter-position is this: one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. Do you think that changes the recommendation?
B: It changes the conditions around it more than the direction. I think we should acknowledge the objection explicitly rather than pretend it is trivial.
A: So what would you recommend as the next step?
B: I would support this outcome: the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators. It gives us a decision without pretending the uncertainty has disappeared.
A: And how should we frame the conclusion for the final document?
B: I would keep one principle visible throughout: reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim.

## Key phrases
- is thought to
- is understood to
- is estimated to
- on the evidence available
- a defensible conclusion

## Comprehension
1. What does Speaker B identify as the first important evidence?
2. What second strand of evidence is mentioned?
3. What limitation prevents a broader conclusion?
4. Does the counterargument completely reverse Speaker B’s recommendation?
5. What outcome does Speaker B support?

## Answers
1. several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter
2. business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized
3. the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters
4. No. It changes the conditions and wording more than the overall direction.
5. the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators

contents.title: Grammar: Impersonal and personal reporting passives
contents.body:
## Why it matters
Reporting passives allow writers to attribute beliefs, expectations, estimates, and reports without always foregrounding the source. They are common in formal genres, but they vary in time reference and evidential force. C1 users should preserve the distinction between what is known, expected, alleged, and estimated.

At C1, Impersonal and personal reporting passives is best treated as a discourse choice rather than an isolated rule. Learners should be able to select the structure according to emphasis, stance, information flow, and register, while retaining reliable control of form. The same proposition can often be expressed in several grammatically possible ways; advanced competence lies in choosing the version that best serves the communicative purpose.

## Form
| Focus | Form | Example |
| impersonal it | It + be + past participle + that-clause | It is expected that inflation will fall modestly. |
| personal reporting passive | subject + be + past participle + to-infinitive | Inflation is expected to fall modestly. |
| prior event | subject + be + past participle + to have + past participle | Costs are believed to have stabilized last quarter. |
| ongoing state/action | subject + be + past participle + to be + -ing/adjective | Demand is thought to be weakening gradually. |

Contrastive noticing should include near-equivalent alternatives. Ask what changes when the sentence is made more personal or impersonal, more categorical or more tentative, more neutral or more rhetorically marked. Learners should justify their selection in terms of meaning and context, not merely identify a memorized pattern.

## Examples
+ Inflation is expected to fall modestly during the next quarter.
+ It is understood that official figures will be released next week.
+ Energy costs are believed to have stabilized recently.
+ Demand is thought to be weakening in several sectors.
- The forecast is not known to be certain simply because many analysts share it.
? Which form would you use for an earlier event: to fall or to have fallen?
? Who exactly is the source in an impersonal reporting passive?
? How should the wording change if the claim is only alleged?

Production practice should move quickly from sentence-level control to connected discourse. A useful sequence is reformulation, expansion, and register shift: first correct or transform a sentence; then embed it in a short argument or narrative; finally rewrite the same idea for a different audience. This reveals whether the grammar remains stable when lexical and pragmatic demands increase.

## Use it / When to use
- Use reporting passives to summarize attributed expectations or beliefs in formal prose.
- Use to have + past participle when the reported event precedes the reporting reference point.
- Choose the reporting participle carefully: expected, believed, reported, alleged, estimated, and known are not interchangeable.
- Name the source when source identity is important to evaluating credibility.
- Do not use an impersonal passive to disguise weak evidence as institutional consensus.

Feedback at this level should address appropriacy as well as grammaticality. A sentence may be formally correct but too emphatic, too vague, too conversational, or unnecessarily dense for the situation. Encourage learners to test alternatives and explain which one creates the intended focus, interpersonal effect, or degree of commitment.

## Common Mistakes
~~Inflation is expected that it will fall.~~ -> Inflation is expected to fall. / It is expected that inflation will fall.
~~Costs are believed to stabilize last quarter.~~ -> Costs are believed to have stabilized last quarter.
~~It is expected inflation to fall.~~ -> It is expected that inflation will fall.
~~The figure is known to maybe fall.~~ -> The figure is expected to fall. / It is possible that the figure will fall.

A useful final check is to ask whether the form changes the proposition, the degree of commitment, the information focus, or merely the style. Advanced accuracy includes knowing when a simpler structure would communicate the idea more efficiently.


In the context of impersonal reporting passives, learners should practise the target structure with lexical material that is sufficiently demanding to make the grammatical choice meaningful. Advanced control is often tested when several pressures operate at once: the speaker must maintain reference, signal stance, manage clause relationships, and preserve an appropriate register. Tasks should therefore include short stretches of connected language rather than a long sequence of decontextualized transformations.

Corpus-informed teaching at advanced levels also benefits from attention to distribution and conventionality. A construction may be theoretically possible but uncommon in the relevant genre, while another may be strongly associated with formal analysis, spoken disagreement, narrative emphasis, or institutional writing. Learners do not need to memorize frequency tables, but they should notice recurring phraseological patterns and the company that grammatical forms tend to keep.

## Quick Recap
- Two main patterns: it-passive and personal passive.
- Use perfect infinitive for prior events.
- Reporting participles differ in stance.
- Source backgrounding does not remove evidential responsibility.
- Name sources when credibility matters.

contents.title: Tasks: Unit 5
contents.body:
## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Impersonal and personal reporting passives naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. In addition, business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. A credible objection is that one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators. This conclusion remains open to revision because reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using impersonal and personal reporting passives where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

## Task 2
Give a 4-minute seminar-style response on drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Synthesize two perspectives, signal your degree of certainty, and reformulate one point for clarity.

## Model answer
Speaker A: I think the first point we should establish is that several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. Speaker B: Agreed, and I would add that business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. Speaker A: Does that justify the strongest possible conclusion? Speaker B: Not quite, because the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. Speaker A: Some colleagues would say that one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. Speaker B: That is a serious objection. I would acknowledge it explicitly, then explain why the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators still seems proportionate. Speaker A: So the conclusion is conditional rather than weak. Speaker B: Exactly. Reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. The wording should communicate that distinction clearly.

## Task 3
Draft a 220–280 word formal proposal, report, or critical review related to drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Control register, paragraph cohesion, and information focus.

## Model answer
Purpose: This document evaluates drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Evidence: Several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. A second relevant consideration is that business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. Limitation: The official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. Counter-position: One drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. Recommendation: The briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators. Rationale: Reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. The proposed wording should remain concise, but it should preserve the distinction between observation, inference, and judgment so that later readers can see why the recommendation was reasonable and what evidence would justify revising it.

contents.title: Reading: When compact technical labels become hard to process
contents.body:
## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about complex noun phrases require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
The case developed within an engineering firm revising a safety manual for mixed specialist and non-specialist users. Responsibility for the judgment rested with the documentation lead, Tarek Shalaby. The decision concerned which dense noun phrases should be kept as technical labels and which should be unpacked into clauses. None of the available positions was absurd, which was precisely why the discussion demanded care. Each option highlighted a different risk: acting too quickly, waiting too long, or communicating a degree of certainty that the evidence did not warrant. Instead of asking which position sounded most confident, participants separated what could be observed directly from what had to be inferred and from what depended on a value judgment about acceptable consequences. The evidential picture was stronger than a single headline figure suggested. One important observation was that specialists understood recurring labels such as high-pressure valve inspection schedule without difficulty. Alongside it, new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun. That combination gave the discussion substance, but it also raised a methodological question: did the two observations independently support the same conclusion, or did they illuminate different parts of the problem? Treating them as interchangeable would have simplified the argument at the cost of accuracy. The review therefore kept their distinct functions visible while considering what they implied together. The most important constraint appeared when the group considered scope rather than direction: rewriting every technical noun phrase as a full clause made the manual much longer and harder to scan. This did not erase the positive findings, but it prevented them from carrying more weight than they could reasonably bear. The team distinguished uncertainty about whether an effect existed from uncertainty about its size, cause, duration, or transfer to another context. That separation made the discussion less dramatic but more informative, because each kind of uncertainty points to a different next step. The strongest objection came from another direction: some engineers argued that users should simply learn the established terminology rather than simplify it. It would have been easy to summarize that view briefly and dismiss it, but the reviewers instead asked what would follow if the objection were partly right. Some parts of the proposal survived unchanged; others required a smaller scale, a later deadline, or a clearer review threshold. This exercise mattered because a conclusion that can absorb a serious objection is generally stronger than one protected by ignoring it. The eventual decision reflected that narrower reasoning: the manual retained stable technical terms but unpacked one-off dense phrases whose internal relationships were not obvious. What made the outcome useful was not only its content but its reversibility. The group specified what future evidence would justify expansion, revision, or withdrawal. In effect, the recommendation became a structured hypothesis about what should happen next rather than a declaration that debate had ended. This made implementation and later evaluation part of the same reasoning process. What the case ultimately demonstrates is that complex noun phrases are efficient when their structure is familiar or transparent; otherwise, expansion can improve comprehension. The quality of an advanced argument often depends on small linguistic distinctions: whether a source claims or demonstrates, whether a result may occur or is expected to occur, whether a limitation narrows scope or undermines validity, and whether a contrast deserves emphasis or only acknowledgement. These choices shape how readers understand responsibility and certainty long after they have forgotten the exact wording of the original evidence. In practical terms, this means editing technical documentation for readers with different levels of specialist knowledge. The challenge is to produce language that survives both immediate use and later scrutiny: clear enough to guide action, qualified enough to remain accurate, and structured enough for another reader to reconstruct the reasoning. That combination of flexibility and accountability is more valuable than surface complexity.

## Key words
| Word | Meaning | Example |
| premodifier | معدِّل قبل الاسم | The team discussed the premodifier because it affected how the evidence and final decision should be interpreted. |
| postmodifier | معدِّل بعد الاسم | The team discussed the postmodifier because it affected how the evidence and final decision should be interpreted. |
| embedded complement | متمم مضمَّن | The unit uses “embedded complement” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |
| head noun | الاسم الرئيس | Alongside it, new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun. |
| modifier stacking | تكديس المعدِّلات | The unit uses “modifier stacking” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |

## Comprehension
1. What decision did the documentation lead, Tarek Shalaby need to make?
2. What was one important strand of evidence?
3. What second strand of evidence supported the discussion?
4. What was the main limitation?
5. What counter-position had to be considered?
6. What practical outcome was reached?

## Answers
1. which dense noun phrases should be kept as technical labels and which should be unpacked into clauses
2. specialists understood recurring labels such as high-pressure valve inspection schedule without difficulty
3. new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun
4. rewriting every technical noun phrase as a full clause made the manual much longer and harder to scan
5. some engineers argued that users should simply learn the established terminology rather than simplify it

## Before you listen
- Listen for the distinction between evidence, limitation, counterargument, and recommendation.
- Notice how the speakers calibrate certainty and disagreement rather than presenting every point categorically.

## Transcript
A: We need to settle the question of which dense noun phrases should be kept as technical labels and which should be unpacked into clauses. What do you see as the strongest evidence?
B: The first point is that specialists understood recurring labels such as high-pressure valve inspection schedule without difficulty. That is more than a single impression.
A: Agreed. Is there independent support, or are we still relying on one type of evidence?
B: There is a second strand: new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun. I would treat the combination as meaningful, though not automatically conclusive.
A: What is the strongest reason not to go further in the wording?
B: The main limitation is that rewriting every technical noun phrase as a full clause made the manual much longer and harder to scan. That affects how broadly we can generalize the conclusion.
A: A counter-position is this: some engineers argued that users should simply learn the established terminology rather than simplify it. Do you think that changes the recommendation?
B: It changes the conditions around it more than the direction. I think we should acknowledge the objection explicitly rather than pretend it is trivial.
A: So what would you recommend as the next step?
B: I would support this outcome: the manual retained stable technical terms but unpacked one-off dense phrases whose internal relationships were not obvious. It gives us a decision without pretending the uncertainty has disappeared.
A: And how should we frame the conclusion for the final document?
B: I would keep one principle visible throughout: complex noun phrases are efficient when their structure is familiar or transparent; otherwise, expansion can improve comprehension.

2. What second strand of evidence is mentioned?
3. What limitation prevents a broader conclusion?
4. Does the counterargument completely reverse Speaker B’s recommendation?
5. What outcome does Speaker B support?

2. new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun
3. rewriting every technical noun phrase as a full clause made the manual much longer and harder to scan

contents.title: Grammar: Complex noun phrases and modifier scope
contents.body:
## Why it matters
Advanced written English often packages information into noun phrases with multiple premodifiers, postmodifiers, complements, and embedded clauses. C1 users need to identify the head noun, control which modifier applies to which element, and decide when unpacking is more readable than further compression.

At C1, Complex noun phrases and modifier scope is best treated as a discourse choice rather than an isolated rule. Learners should be able to select the structure according to emphasis, stance, information flow, and register, while retaining reliable control of form. The same proposition can often be expressed in several grammatically possible ways; advanced competence lies in choosing the version that best serves the communicative purpose.

## Form
| Focus | Form | Example |
| premodification | modifier(s) + head noun | high-pressure valve inspection schedule |
| postmodification | head noun + prepositional/relative phrase | the schedule for valves used in high-pressure systems |
| noun complement | head noun + that-clause/of-phrase | the assumption that all staff know the procedure |
| mixed complex NP | premodifiers + head + postmodifier | the revised emergency shutdown procedure for new laboratory staff |

Contrastive noticing should include near-equivalent alternatives. Ask what changes when the sentence is made more personal or impersonal, more categorical or more tentative, more neutral or more rhetorically marked. Learners should justify their selection in terms of meaning and context, not merely identify a memorized pattern.

## Examples
+ The manual retained the established high-pressure valve inspection schedule.
+ New staff received guidance on the procedure for equipment used in restricted areas.
+ The assumption that all users understood the label proved unsafe.
+ The revised emergency shutdown procedure for new laboratory staff was easier to follow.
- The editors did not preserve a dense noun string whose internal relationships were unclear.
? What is the head noun in “revised equipment maintenance reporting procedure”?
? Which modifier does “for new staff” attach to in the sentence?
? When should a noun phrase be unpacked into a clause?

Production practice should move quickly from sentence-level control to connected discourse. A useful sequence is reformulation, expansion, and register shift: first correct or transform a sentence; then embed it in a short argument or narrative; finally rewrite the same idea for a different audience. This reveals whether the grammar remains stable when lexical and pragmatic demands increase.

## Use it / When to use
- Identify the head noun before interpreting a long noun phrase.
- Keep established technical terms compact when readers reliably recognize them.
- Use postmodifiers to clarify relations that would be ambiguous in a long noun string.
- Unpack hidden causal or temporal relations into clauses when they matter to interpretation.
- Avoid stacking modifiers whose scope a reader must guess.

Feedback at this level should address appropriacy as well as grammaticality. A sentence may be formally correct but too emphatic, too vague, too conversational, or unnecessarily dense for the situation. Encourage learners to test alternatives and explain which one creates the intended focus, interpersonal effect, or degree of commitment.

## Common Mistakes
~~the safety high pressure valve schedule inspection~~ -> the high-pressure valve inspection schedule
~~the assumption all staff know the procedure~~ -> the assumption that all staff know the procedure
~~the revised for new staff emergency procedure~~ -> the revised emergency procedure for new staff
~~the system failure prevention rapid response protocol team~~ -> the team’s rapid-response protocol for preventing system failure

A useful final check is to ask whether the form changes the proposition, the degree of commitment, the information focus, or merely the style. Advanced accuracy includes knowing when a simpler structure would communicate the idea more efficiently.


In the context of complex noun phrases, learners should practise the target structure with lexical material that is sufficiently demanding to make the grammatical choice meaningful. Advanced control is often tested when several pressures operate at once: the speaker must maintain reference, signal stance, manage clause relationships, and preserve an appropriate register. Tasks should therefore include short stretches of connected language rather than a long sequence of decontextualized transformations.

Corpus-informed teaching at advanced levels also benefits from attention to distribution and conventionality. A construction may be theoretically possible but uncommon in the relevant genre, while another may be strongly associated with formal analysis, spoken disagreement, narrative emphasis, or institutional writing. Learners do not need to memorize frequency tables, but they should notice recurring phraseological patterns and the company that grammatical forms tend to keep.

Editing work should distinguish error from preference. First correct forms that are ungrammatical or that distort the intended meaning. Then consider whether a more idiomatic, concise, or audience-sensitive alternative would improve the text. This two-stage process protects accuracy while acknowledging that advanced English often allows multiple acceptable formulations with different rhetorical effects.

## Quick Recap
- Find the head noun first.
- Premodifiers are compact but can become ambiguous.
- Postmodifiers often clarify relationships.
- Noun complements may use that-clauses.
- Unpack when processing cost becomes too high.

contents.title: Tasks: Unit 6
contents.body:
## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating editing technical documentation for readers with different levels of specialist knowledge. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Complex noun phrases and modifier scope naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on editing technical documentation for readers with different levels of specialist knowledge requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that specialists understood recurring labels such as high-pressure valve inspection schedule without difficulty. In addition, new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because rewriting every technical noun phrase as a full clause made the manual much longer and harder to scan. A credible objection is that some engineers argued that users should simply learn the established terminology rather than simplify it. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the manual retained stable technical terms but unpacked one-off dense phrases whose internal relationships were not obvious. This conclusion remains open to revision because complex noun phrases are efficient when their structure is familiar or transparent; otherwise, expansion can improve comprehension. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using complex noun phrases and modifier scope where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

## Task 2
Give a 4-minute seminar-style response on editing technical documentation for readers with different levels of specialist knowledge. Synthesize two perspectives, signal your degree of certainty, and reformulate one point for clarity.

## Model answer
Speaker A: I think the first point we should establish is that specialists understood recurring labels such as high-pressure valve inspection schedule without difficulty. Speaker B: Agreed, and I would add that new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun. Speaker A: Does that justify the strongest possible conclusion? Speaker B: Not quite, because rewriting every technical noun phrase as a full clause made the manual much longer and harder to scan. Speaker A: Some colleagues would say that some engineers argued that users should simply learn the established terminology rather than simplify it. Speaker B: That is a serious objection. I would acknowledge it explicitly, then explain why the manual retained stable technical terms but unpacked one-off dense phrases whose internal relationships were not obvious still seems proportionate. Speaker A: So the conclusion is conditional rather than weak. Speaker B: Exactly. Complex noun phrases are efficient when their structure is familiar or transparent; otherwise, expansion can improve comprehension. The wording should communicate that distinction clearly.

## Task 3
Draft a 220–280 word formal proposal, report, or critical review related to editing technical documentation for readers with different levels of specialist knowledge. Control register, paragraph cohesion, and information focus.

## Model answer
Purpose: This document evaluates editing technical documentation for readers with different levels of specialist knowledge. Evidence: Specialists understood recurring labels such as high-pressure valve inspection schedule without difficulty. A second relevant consideration is that new staff struggled with longer strings containing several premodifiers and postmodifiers before reaching the head noun. Limitation: Rewriting every technical noun phrase as a full clause made the manual much longer and harder to scan. Counter-position: Some engineers argued that users should simply learn the established terminology rather than simplify it. Recommendation: The manual retained stable technical terms but unpacked one-off dense phrases whose internal relationships were not obvious. Rationale: Complex noun phrases are efficient when their structure is familiar or transparent; otherwise, expansion can improve comprehension. The proposed wording should remain concise, but it should preserve the distinction between observation, inference, and judgment so that later readers can see why the recommendation was reasonable and what evidence would justify revising it.

contents.title: Reading: A report that was accurate sentence by sentence but difficult as a whole
contents.body:
## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about cohesion, reference & text flow require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
A review took place within a policy institute reviewing a long comparative report on urban transport. The central responsibility lay with the review editor, Leila Osman. The question was how to improve cohesion without adding repetitive signposting to every paragraph. The disagreement was not simply between people who supported or opposed change. It concerned the structure of the reasoning: which facts were established, which interpretations were plausible, and which claims rested on assumptions that had not yet been tested. Because the eventual document would guide action, the group needed a formulation useful enough to support a decision yet restrained enough to remain defensible under later scrutiny. The case for action did not rest on one dramatic fact. It drew first on the finding that individual sentences were grammatically accurate and the data tables were well labeled, and then on the additional observation that readers frequently lost track of which city, proposal, or dataset pronouns and demonstratives referred to after several paragraphs. Together, these points shifted the burden of discussion: opponents could no longer say that nothing meaningful had changed. Even so, the evidence answered some questions better than others. It could establish a pattern more confidently than a cause, and it could support a local decision more readily than a universal conclusion. One feature prevented a simple conclusion: replacing every reference with a full noun phrase made the prose heavy and repetitive. The group treated this as a boundary condition rather than a reason to abandon the analysis. What changed was the grammar of the claim—from broad certainty to a conclusion tied to the population, period, source, or mechanism actually studied. That kind of qualification is not a retreat from decision-making. It is a way of preventing a local result from being silently converted into a general law. Not everyone accepted the emerging interpretation. A competing view held that one analyst argued that sophisticated readers should be able to infer the intended reference from context. The disagreement proved useful because it forced the group to identify which premise actually separated the two positions. Once that premise was visible, participants could ask what evidence would confirm or weaken it. The debate therefore moved away from preference and toward a testable difference in assumptions, reducing the temptation to treat confidence of delivery as evidence of correctness. The review concluded with a proportionate step: the revision strengthened lexical chains, reset key nouns at strategic points, and used devices such as thereby and the former selectively. The decision did not eliminate uncertainty, nor did it postpone action until uncertainty disappeared. Instead, it matched the scale of commitment to the strength of the present evidence. The written record also preserved the assumptions behind the choice, making future disagreement easier to resolve. If conditions changed, reviewers would be able to ask whether the original reasoning had failed or whether the context itself had moved. The underlying principle can be stated simply: cohesion depends on recoverable reference and logical continuity, not on maximizing the number of linking expressions. Applying it, however, requires control over more than vocabulary difficulty. Writers need to manage reference, evidential distance, clause relationships, information focus, and the social force of disagreement. A sophisticated sentence is one whose form earns its place by improving those functions. When a simpler structure does the job more transparently, choosing the simpler structure is itself evidence of advanced control. The communicative challenge is therefore revising an analytical report whose local sentences are correct but whose global flow is difficult to follow. Success depends on preserving the relation between evidence and claim while still producing a usable conclusion. An expert reader should be able to see not only what was decided, but why that wording was chosen, which alternatives were considered, and which future observations would reopen the question.

## Key words
| Word | Meaning | Example |
| thereby | وبذلك | Choose connectors such as thereby and hence according to logical relation, not as general-purpose formal markers. |
| hence | ومن ثم | The speaker used hence to signal a precise relationship of stance, degree, timing, or discourse in context. |
| the former | الأول منهما | + The report compared two proposals; the former focused on cost, while the latter prioritized access. |
| the latter | الثاني منهما | The unit uses “the latter” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |
| referential chain | سلسلة إحالية | The unit uses “referential chain” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |

## Comprehension
1. What decision did the review editor, Leila Osman need to make?
2. What was one important strand of evidence?
3. What second strand of evidence supported the discussion?
4. What was the main limitation?
5. What counter-position had to be considered?
6. What practical outcome was reached?

## Answers
1. how to improve cohesion without adding repetitive signposting to every paragraph
2. individual sentences were grammatically accurate and the data tables were well labeled
3. readers frequently lost track of which city, proposal, or dataset pronouns and demonstratives referred to after several paragraphs
4. replacing every reference with a full noun phrase made the prose heavy and repetitive
5. one analyst argued that sophisticated readers should be able to infer the intended reference from context
6. the revision strengthened lexical chains, reset key nouns at strategic points, and used devices such as thereby and the former selectively

## Before you listen
- Listen for the distinction between evidence, limitation, counterargument, and recommendation.
- Notice how the speakers calibrate certainty and disagreement rather than presenting every point categorically.

## Transcript

B: The first point is that individual sentences were grammatically accurate and the data tables were well labeled. That is more than a single impression.

B: There is a second strand: readers frequently lost track of which city, proposal, or dataset pronouns and demonstratives referred to after several paragraphs. I would treat the combination as meaningful, though not automatically conclusive.

contents.title: Grammar: Advanced cohesion and reference tracking
contents.body:
## Why it matters
Cohesion links stretches of discourse through reference, lexical repetition and variation, substitution, and logical signaling. At C1, users should maintain clear chains of reference over multiple sentences and know when a pronoun, demonstrative, or compressed label has become too distant or ambiguous.

At C1, Advanced cohesion and reference tracking is best treated as a discourse choice rather than an isolated rule. Learners should be able to select the structure according to emphasis, stance, information flow, and register, while retaining reliable control of form. The same proposition can often be expressed in several grammatically possible ways; advanced competence lies in choosing the version that best serves the communicative purpose.

## Form
| Focus | Form | Example |
| anaphoric reference | pronoun/demonstrative → earlier referent | The proposal was revised. This reduced cost. |
| cataphoric reference | reference → later specification | This was the central problem: no branch used the system in the same way. |
| lexical chain | related nouns/phrases across text | proposal → plan → revised scheme |
| consequential link | clause; thereby/hence + result | The team clarified the categories, thereby reducing ambiguity. |

Contrastive noticing should include near-equivalent alternatives. Ask what changes when the sentence is made more personal or impersonal, more categorical or more tentative, more neutral or more rhetorically marked. Learners should justify their selection in terms of meaning and context, not merely identify a memorized pattern.

## Examples
+ The report compared two proposals; the former focused on cost, while the latter prioritized access.
+ The categories were clarified, thereby reducing reference ambiguity.
+ This was the main difficulty: readers could not identify which city the pronoun referred to.
+ The revised scheme retained the central proposal but changed its funding model.
- The editor did not replace every noun with a pronoun merely to avoid repetition.
? What does the former refer to when two proposals have just been named?
? Why might a repeated key noun be clearer than another pronoun?
? Which device expresses a result in “thereby reducing ambiguity”?

Production practice should move quickly from sentence-level control to connected discourse. A useful sequence is reformulation, expansion, and register shift: first correct or transform a sentence; then embed it in a short argument or narrative; finally rewrite the same idea for a different audience. This reveals whether the grammar remains stable when lexical and pragmatic demands increase.

## Use it / When to use
- Use pronouns and demonstratives only while the intended referent remains salient.
- Reset a full noun phrase when several competing referents have intervened.
- Use lexical chains to create continuity without mechanical repetition.
- Use former/latter only when exactly two clearly ordered referents are easy to recover.
- Choose connectors such as thereby and hence according to logical relation, not as general-purpose formal markers.

Feedback at this level should address appropriacy as well as grammaticality. A sentence may be formally correct but too emphatic, too vague, too conversational, or unnecessarily dense for the situation. Encourage learners to test alternatives and explain which one creates the intended focus, interpersonal effect, or degree of commitment.

## Common Mistakes
~~Three proposals were discussed; the former was cheapest.~~ -> Three proposals were discussed; the first was cheapest.
~~The policy changed. Which reduced confusion.~~ -> The policy changed, which reduced confusion. / The policy changed. This reduced confusion.
~~The first and second plans differed; the latter of the three was cheaper.~~ -> The first and second plans differed; the latter was cheaper.
~~The editor clarified the labels, thereby the readers understood them.~~ -> The editor clarified the labels, thereby helping readers understand them.

A useful final check is to ask whether the form changes the proposition, the degree of commitment, the information focus, or merely the style. Advanced accuracy includes knowing when a simpler structure would communicate the idea more efficiently.


In the context of cohesion, reference & text flow, learners should practise the target structure with lexical material that is sufficiently demanding to make the grammatical choice meaningful. Advanced control is often tested when several pressures operate at once: the speaker must maintain reference, signal stance, manage clause relationships, and preserve an appropriate register. Tasks should therefore include short stretches of connected language rather than a long sequence of decontextualized transformations.

Corpus-informed teaching at advanced levels also benefits from attention to distribution and conventionality. A construction may be theoretically possible but uncommon in the relevant genre, while another may be strongly associated with formal analysis, spoken disagreement, narrative emphasis, or institutional writing. Learners do not need to memorize frequency tables, but they should notice recurring phraseological patterns and the company that grammatical forms tend to keep.

## Quick Recap
- Cohesion requires recoverable reference.
- Former/latter work best with exactly two referents.
- Lexical repetition can be useful.
- Thereby commonly introduces a consequence in a non-finite phrase.
- Global flow matters beyond sentence-level correctness.

contents.title: Tasks: Unit 7
contents.body:
## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating revising an analytical report whose local sentences are correct but whose global flow is difficult to follow. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Advanced cohesion and reference tracking naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on revising an analytical report whose local sentences are correct but whose global flow is difficult to follow requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that individual sentences were grammatically accurate and the data tables were well labeled. In addition, readers frequently lost track of which city, proposal, or dataset pronouns and demonstratives referred to after several paragraphs. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because replacing every reference with a full noun phrase made the prose heavy and repetitive. A credible objection is that one analyst argued that sophisticated readers should be able to infer the intended reference from context. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the revision strengthened lexical chains, reset key nouns at strategic points, and used devices such as thereby and the former selectively. This conclusion remains open to revision because cohesion depends on recoverable reference and logical continuity, not on maximizing the number of linking expressions. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using advanced cohesion and reference tracking where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

## Task 2
Give a 4-minute seminar-style response on revising an analytical report whose local sentences are correct but whose global flow is difficult to follow. Synthesize two perspectives, signal your degree of certainty, and reformulate one point for clarity.

## Model answer
Speaker A: I think the first point we should establish is that individual sentences were grammatically accurate and the data tables were well labeled. Speaker B: Agreed, and I would add that readers frequently lost track of which city, proposal, or dataset pronouns and demonstratives referred to after several paragraphs. Speaker A: Does that justify the strongest possible conclusion? Speaker B: Not quite, because replacing every reference with a full noun phrase made the prose heavy and repetitive. Speaker A: Some colleagues would say that one analyst argued that sophisticated readers should be able to infer the intended reference from context. Speaker B: That is a serious objection. I would acknowledge it explicitly, then explain why the revision strengthened lexical chains, reset key nouns at strategic points, and used devices such as thereby and the former selectively still seems proportionate. Speaker A: So the conclusion is conditional rather than weak. Speaker B: Exactly. Cohesion depends on recoverable reference and logical continuity, not on maximizing the number of linking expressions. The wording should communicate that distinction clearly.

## Task 3
Draft a 220–280 word formal proposal, report, or critical review related to revising an analytical report whose local sentences are correct but whose global flow is difficult to follow. Control register, paragraph cohesion, and information focus.

## Model answer
Purpose: This document evaluates revising an analytical report whose local sentences are correct but whose global flow is difficult to follow. Evidence: Individual sentences were grammatically accurate and the data tables were well labeled. A second relevant consideration is that readers frequently lost track of which city, proposal, or dataset pronouns and demonstratives referred to after several paragraphs. Limitation: Replacing every reference with a full noun phrase made the prose heavy and repetitive. Counter-position: One analyst argued that sophisticated readers should be able to infer the intended reference from context. Recommendation: The revision strengthened lexical chains, reset key nouns at strategic points, and used devices such as thereby and the former selectively. Rationale: Cohesion depends on recoverable reference and logical continuity, not on maximizing the number of linking expressions. The proposed wording should remain concise, but it should preserve the distinction between observation, inference, and judgment so that later readers can see why the recommendation was reasonable and what evidence would justify revising it.

contents.title: Reading: Why the same request can sound efficient or abrasive
contents.body:
## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about register, politeness & mitigation require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
A review was conducted within an international project team comparing email styles across departments. It was led by the project coordinator, Nour ElDin. The central question was how direct internal messages should be when deadlines are tight but relationships remain important. At first, several participants treated the issue as a contest between competing conclusions. The discussion changed once they recognized that the arguments operated at different levels. Some described measurable outcomes, others predicted future effects, and still others reflected values about what should count as an acceptable risk. A reliable conclusion would have to keep those levels distinct while still producing a practical recommendation rather than an elegant description of uncertainty. Rather than rely on a single indicator, the review compared two different sources of support. The first strand was clear: short imperative messages were efficient among close colleagues who shared responsibilities and context. The second added another perspective: the same forms were interpreted as abrupt when sent to external partners or senior stakeholders with less shared background. The combination was persuasive precisely because the sources approached the issue from different angles. Yet difference also limited easy aggregation. A coherent synthesis had to preserve what each source measured instead of treating all favorable information as though it were one undifferentiated quantity of proof. A closer reading exposed an important limitation: overly elaborate politeness sometimes hid the actual request and delayed action. The implication was not that the evidence had become worthless, but that the inference needed a narrower domain. Reviewers mapped which parts of the conclusion were directly observed, which depended on extrapolation, and which were judgments about acceptable risk. Once those layers were separated, it became easier to say both what the evidence supported and what further information would genuinely change the decision. The analysis also had to confront a politically or practically attractive alternative: some team members argued that direct language was always clearer and therefore professionally superior. Rather than frame the dispute as caution versus ambition, the group compared the consequences of being wrong in each direction. That reframing showed that the counter-position contained a legitimate concern even where its preferred conclusion did not follow. The final recommendation therefore incorporated part of the objection without surrendering distinctions that the evidence still required. The final position was deliberately conditional in scope: the team adopted flexible guidance: state the action clearly, then calibrate mitigation according to relationship, burden, and urgency. This allowed the organization to act while keeping its evidential commitments visible. Rather than present the recommendation as the inevitable consequence of the data, the document showed how evidence, limitation, counterargument, and institutional priorities combined. That distinction matters because later readers often remember conclusions more clearly than the qualifications that made them reasonable. The case therefore supports a broader proposition: advanced politeness is not indirectness for its own sake; it is the ability to manage clarity and interpersonal impact simultaneously. That proposition links analysis with communication. Decisions become harder to audit when language hides who made an inference, where a number came from, or how much uncertainty remains. Conversely, careful wording can make disagreement productive by showing exactly which premise, source, or risk judgment needs to be challenged. Precision is not cosmetic; it is part of responsible reasoning. The same discipline applies when the task becomes rewriting professional requests and disagreements for different relationships and levels of urgency. A proficient response does not hide complexity, but neither does it make complexity the reader’s problem. It organizes the relevant distinctions, calibrates commitment, and leaves a clear path from evidence to action. That is the point at which linguistic sophistication becomes functional rather than ornamental.

## Key words
| Word | Meaning | Example |
| deference | مراعاة المقام والاحترام | The team discussed the deference because it affected how the evidence and final decision should be interpreted. |
| soften a request | يلطّف طلبًا | The analyst chose to soften a request only after reviewing the evidence, assumptions, and likely consequences carefully. |
| face-saving | حفظ ماء الوجه | The team discussed the face-saving because it affected how the evidence and final decision should be interpreted. |
| imposition | عبء أو إملاء على المخاطب | The team discussed the imposition because it affected how the evidence and final decision should be interpreted. |
| diplomatic wording | صياغة دبلوماسية | The unit uses “diplomatic wording” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |

## Comprehension
1. What decision did the project coordinator, Nour ElDin need to make?
2. What was one important strand of evidence?
3. What second strand of evidence supported the discussion?
4. What was the main limitation?
5. What counter-position had to be considered?
6. What practical outcome was reached?

## Answers
1. how direct internal messages should be when deadlines are tight but relationships remain important
2. short imperative messages were efficient among close colleagues who shared responsibilities and context
3. the same forms were interpreted as abrupt when sent to external partners or senior stakeholders with less shared background
4. overly elaborate politeness sometimes hid the actual request and delayed action
5. some team members argued that direct language was always clearer and therefore professionally superior
6. the team adopted flexible guidance: state the action clearly, then calibrate mitigation according to relationship, burden, and urgency

contents.title: Listening: Is this clear enough, or too blunt?
contents.body:
## Before you listen
- Listen for the distinction between evidence, limitation, counterargument, and recommendation.
- Notice how the speakers calibrate certainty and disagreement rather than presenting every point categorically.

## Transcript
A: We need to settle the question of how direct internal messages should be when deadlines are tight but relationships remain important. What do you see as the strongest evidence?
B: The first point is that short imperative messages were efficient among close colleagues who shared responsibilities and context. That is more than a single impression.
A: Agreed. Is there independent support, or are we still relying on one type of evidence?
B: There is a second strand: the same forms were interpreted as abrupt when sent to external partners or senior stakeholders with less shared background. I would treat the combination as meaningful, though not automatically conclusive.
A: What is the strongest reason not to go further in the wording?
B: The main limitation is that overly elaborate politeness sometimes hid the actual request and delayed action. That affects how broadly we can generalize the conclusion.
A: A counter-position is this: some team members argued that direct language was always clearer and therefore professionally superior. Do you think that changes the recommendation?
B: It changes the conditions around it more than the direction. I think we should acknowledge the objection explicitly rather than pretend it is trivial.
A: So what would you recommend as the next step?
B: I would support this outcome: the team adopted flexible guidance: state the action clearly, then calibrate mitigation according to relationship, burden, and urgency. It gives us a decision without pretending the uncertainty has disappeared.
A: And how should we frame the conclusion for the final document?
B: I would keep one principle visible throughout: advanced politeness is not indirectness for its own sake; it is the ability to manage clarity and interpersonal impact simultaneously.

## Key phrases
- deference
- soften a request
- face-saving
- on the evidence available
- a defensible conclusion

## Comprehension
1. What does Speaker B identify as the first important evidence?
2. What second strand of evidence is mentioned?
3. What limitation prevents a broader conclusion?
4. Does the counterargument completely reverse Speaker B’s recommendation?
5. What outcome does Speaker B support?

## Answers
1. short imperative messages were efficient among close colleagues who shared responsibilities and context
2. the same forms were interpreted as abrupt when sent to external partners or senior stakeholders with less shared background
3. overly elaborate politeness sometimes hid the actual request and delayed action
4. No. It changes the conditions and wording more than the overall direction.
5. the team adopted flexible guidance: state the action clearly, then calibrate mitigation according to relationship, burden, and urgency

contents.title: Grammar: Register, mitigation and interpersonal stance
contents.body:
## Why it matters
Advanced users need to adjust directness to relationship, hierarchy, burden, urgency, and genre. Mitigation can be expressed through modals, conditionals, past forms, stance frames, and lexical choices. The goal is neither maximum politeness nor maximum directness, but an appropriate balance between clarity and interpersonal effect.

At C1, Register, mitigation and interpersonal stance is best treated as a discourse choice rather than an isolated rule. Learners should be able to select the structure according to emphasis, stance, information flow, and register, while retaining reliable control of form. The same proposition can often be expressed in several grammatically possible ways; advanced competence lies in choosing the version that best serves the communicative purpose.

## Form
| Focus | Form | Example |
| modal request | Could/Would you + base...? | Could you send the revised figures by noon? |
| conditional softener | I would appreciate it if + past | I would appreciate it if you could confirm the deadline. |
| tentative suggestion | It might be worth + -ing | It might be worth reviewing the wording before publication. |
| diplomatic disagreement | I’m not sure I would + base / I wonder whether | I’m not sure I would describe the evidence as conclusive. |

Contrastive noticing should include near-equivalent alternatives. Ask what changes when the sentence is made more personal or impersonal, more categorical or more tentative, more neutral or more rhetorically marked. Learners should justify their selection in terms of meaning and context, not merely identify a memorized pattern.

## Examples
+ Could you confirm which version should be sent to the external partner?
+ I would appreciate it if you could send the revised figures by noon.
+ It might be worth explaining the reason for the delay in the opening line.
+ I’m not sure I would characterize the request as optional.
- The message should not become so indirect that the required action is impossible to identify.
? How would you make this request more appropriate for an external senior partner?
? When might a direct imperative be entirely acceptable?
? Which wording challenges a claim without directly attacking the speaker?

Production practice should move quickly from sentence-level control to connected discourse. A useful sequence is reformulation, expansion, and register shift: first correct or transform a sentence; then embed it in a short argument or narrative; finally rewrite the same idea for a different audience. This reveals whether the grammar remains stable when lexical and pragmatic demands increase.

## Use it / When to use
- Calibrate mitigation to social distance, power relationship, burden, and urgency.
- Use modals and conditional frames for requests that impose on the recipient.
- Use tentative stance frames to disagree with a formulation while keeping discussion open.
- Keep the requested action explicit even in highly polite messages.
- Do not assume directness is rude or indirectness is polite independent of context.

Feedback at this level should address appropriacy as well as grammaticality. A sentence may be formally correct but too emphatic, too vague, too conversational, or unnecessarily dense for the situation. Encourage learners to test alternatives and explain which one creates the intended focus, interpersonal effect, or degree of commitment.

## Common Mistakes
~~I would appreciate if you send the figures.~~ -> I would appreciate it if you could send the figures.
~~It might worth reviewing the wording.~~ -> It might be worth reviewing the wording.
~~Could you to confirm the date?~~ -> Could you confirm the date?
~~I am not sure I would described it as conclusive.~~ -> I’m not sure I would describe it as conclusive.

A useful final check is to ask whether the form changes the proposition, the degree of commitment, the information focus, or merely the style. Advanced accuracy includes knowing when a simpler structure would communicate the idea more efficiently.


In the context of register, politeness & mitigation, learners should practise the target structure with lexical material that is sufficiently demanding to make the grammatical choice meaningful. Advanced control is often tested when several pressures operate at once: the speaker must maintain reference, signal stance, manage clause relationships, and preserve an appropriate register. Tasks should therefore include short stretches of connected language rather than a long sequence of decontextualized transformations.

Corpus-informed teaching at advanced levels also benefits from attention to distribution and conventionality. A construction may be theoretically possible but uncommon in the relevant genre, while another may be strongly associated with formal analysis, spoken disagreement, narrative emphasis, or institutional writing. Learners do not need to memorize frequency tables, but they should notice recurring phraseological patterns and the company that grammatical forms tend to keep.

## Quick Recap
- Register is context-dependent.
- Mitigation can reduce interpersonal force.
- Clarity remains essential.
- Past and modal forms can create distance.
- Directness and politeness are not opposites in every context.

contents.title: Tasks: Unit 8
contents.body:
## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating rewriting professional requests and disagreements for different relationships and levels of urgency. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Register, mitigation and interpersonal stance naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on rewriting professional requests and disagreements for different relationships and levels of urgency requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that short imperative messages were efficient among close colleagues who shared responsibilities and context. In addition, the same forms were interpreted as abrupt when sent to external partners or senior stakeholders with less shared background. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because overly elaborate politeness sometimes hid the actual request and delayed action. A credible objection is that some team members argued that direct language was always clearer and therefore professionally superior. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the team adopted flexible guidance: state the action clearly, then calibrate mitigation according to relationship, burden, and urgency. This conclusion remains open to revision because advanced politeness is not indirectness for its own sake; it is the ability to manage clarity and interpersonal impact simultaneously. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using register, mitigation and interpersonal stance where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

## Task 2
Give a 4-minute seminar-style response on rewriting professional requests and disagreements for different relationships and levels of urgency. Synthesize two perspectives, signal your degree of certainty, and reformulate one point for clarity.

## Model answer
Speaker A: I think the first point we should establish is that short imperative messages were efficient among close colleagues who shared responsibilities and context. Speaker B: Agreed, and I would add that the same forms were interpreted as abrupt when sent to external partners or senior stakeholders with less shared background. Speaker A: Does that justify the strongest possible conclusion? Speaker B: Not quite, because overly elaborate politeness sometimes hid the actual request and delayed action. Speaker A: Some colleagues would say that some team members argued that direct language was always clearer and therefore professionally superior. Speaker B: That is a serious objection. I would acknowledge it explicitly, then explain why the team adopted flexible guidance: state the action clearly, then calibrate mitigation according to relationship, burden, and urgency still seems proportionate. Speaker A: So the conclusion is conditional rather than weak. Speaker B: Exactly. Advanced politeness is not indirectness for its own sake; it is the ability to manage clarity and interpersonal impact simultaneously. The wording should communicate that distinction clearly.

## Task 3
Draft a 220–280 word formal proposal, report, or critical review related to rewriting professional requests and disagreements for different relationships and levels of urgency. Control register, paragraph cohesion, and information focus.

## Model answer
Purpose: This document evaluates rewriting professional requests and disagreements for different relationships and levels of urgency. Evidence: Short imperative messages were efficient among close colleagues who shared responsibilities and context. A second relevant consideration is that the same forms were interpreted as abrupt when sent to external partners or senior stakeholders with less shared background. Limitation: Overly elaborate politeness sometimes hid the actual request and delayed action. Counter-position: Some team members argued that direct language was always clearer and therefore professionally superior. Recommendation: The team adopted flexible guidance: state the action clearly, then calibrate mitigation according to relationship, burden, and urgency. Rationale: Advanced politeness is not indirectness for its own sake; it is the ability to manage clarity and interpersonal impact simultaneously. The proposed wording should remain concise, but it should preserve the distinction between observation, inference, and judgment so that later readers can see why the recommendation was reasonable and what evidence would justify revising it.
